resources.title: The Paris Peace Accords, 1973

content.topicNotes: The Paris Peace Accords, 1973 The Paris Peace Accords were signed in 1973 and included the following agreements. Signatories The Paris Peace Accords were signed by:The USA. North Vietnam. South Vietnam. The National Liberation Front (now called the Provisional Revolutionary Government). They all agreed to: Reunification and ceasefire Accept the reunification of Vietnam and a new government to be elected with international supervision. Begin a ceasefire between all four of them. Military futures Keep the armies of both South Vietnamese ‘governments’ but the USA would not send aid to the ARVN. Dismantle all US military bases and withdraw all troops, equipment and advisors within 60 days. POWs and aid Exchange prisoners of war and captured equipment within 60 days. The USA to give aid for reconstruction to both sides. Future role of the USA The USA government could not interfere in any way in Vietnam; politically, militarily or otherwise. The Paris Peace Accords, 1973 The Paris Peace Accords did not bring instant peace. Unification only began after the fall of Saigon to the North Vietnamese on 30th April 1975. Military personnel By March 1973 only 150 US marines remained in South Vietnam to guard the US embassy. 10,000 military personnel also remained as civilian advisors. American support Congress cut funding, and most of the aid Nixon had promised to the South did not arrive, leaving the ARVN badly supplied. This led to the collapse of the South Vietnamese economy. Thieu Thieu failed to make the government more democratic or replace corrupt officials, so the popularity of the VC in the villages began to rise again. Thieu refused to negotiate or work with communists; either the North Vietnamese or the Provisional Revolutionary Government. 1974 attack The North grew frustrated with Thieu and launched a new attack in December 1974 using the Ho Chi Minh Trail. The ARVN were unable to fight back, and the USA didn’t send the help they had promised in the case of an attack. Congress only allowed funding to evacuate US citizens. The fall of Saigon The fall of Saigon to the North Vietnamese on 30th April 1975 came much sooner than expected. Vietnam would become a united, communist country. Why did the South Vietnamese economy collapse in 1973? Congress cut funding, and most of the aid Nixon had promised to the South did not arrive, leaving the ARVN badly supplied. This led to the collapse of the South Vietnamese economy.

resources.title: The Polish Crisis & the Outbreak of War

content.topicNotes: Invasion of Poland, 1939 On the 1st September 1939 Poland was invaded by Germany. Invasion of Poland Hitler invaded Poland with force after blowing up the port of Danzig and sending his army and air force into the country. 2 days later, Britain issued an ultimatum to Germany: Withdraw your troops or face a declaration of war. Declaring war The Germans were given a deadline to do this which was ignored. Britain then declared war on Germany, followed by the same declaration from France. Hitler Within 4 weeks, Hitler took all of Poland. Breaking the Treaty of Versailles, the Nazi-Soviet Pact and ignoring the ultimatum from France and Great Britain. The Second World War Hitler thought the threat of war from France and Great Britain wouldn’t amount to anything and they would back down. However, France and Great Britain didn’t back down the Second World War began. The Second World War Hitler thought the threat of war from France and Great Britain wouldn’t amount to anything and they would back down. However, France and Great Britain didn’t back down the Second World War began. Pact of Steel, 1939 In 1939 the Pact of Steel was signed. 1939 In 1939 the Pact of Steel was signed. Allies This was a formal pact joining Germany and Italy as three allies in World War Two.

resources.title: The Responsibility for Cold War Tensions

content.topicNotes: Blaming the Soviet Union for the Cold War The ‘orthodox’ (traditional) interpretation placed the blame for the Cold War tensions on the Soviet Union and its aggressive expansion. US government historians This was a view commonly held by historians who had been involved with the US government. including George Kennan and Herbert Feis These historians pointed to Stalin’s expansionist rhetoric as evidence for these views. 'Red Scare' historians This was a common view among English-speaking historians during the time of the Cold War. And particularly among those who had lived through the ‘Red Scare’. The 'Red Scare' was the fear that communism would spread from within the West and bring down capitalism. Blaming the US Government for the Cold War ‘Revisionists’, prominent from the mid-1960s to the 1970s, were more critical of the US government, particularly given the scandals of the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Vietnam War. Revisionists Revisionists believed that the USA had done little to directly aid the USSR during and immediately after WWII. They believed that the USA had used Marshall Aid as a way to achieve domination over Europe. Forcing the Soviets to behave defensively. Opposite of orthodox This was a direct challenge to the views of orthodox historians. Orthodox historians believed that the USSR was to blame for Cold War tensions.

resources.title: The Rome-Berlin Axis

content.topicNotes: The Rome-Berlin Axis In 1936, Germany and Italy signed an alliance. 1936 As a result of Hitler’s display of strength over the re-occupying of the Rhineland, Mussolini signed a treaty to support Hitler. Both countries promised that they would work closely together. This was the Rome-Berlin Axis. Mussolini's motivations Mussolini was a Fascist like Hitler and wanted a strong military dictatorship in his own country. He also wanted to build an empire (like the previous Roman Empire) so allied with Hitler to do this. Spanish alliance Hitler also had potential allies with Spain as they were also under right-wing government. In 1936 they had a civil war and Hitler supported the Fascist leader Franco by sending the German air force (Luftwaffe) to help support him. He also sent troops to help Franco win. Reassurance Hitler could have used Franco as an ally so this could have possibly motivated him to continually break the rules of the Treaty of Versailles.

resources.title: The Saar

content.topicNotes: Hitler's Actions 1933-1935 In 1933, Germany left the League of Nations. By 1935, Hitler held the ‘Freedom to Rearm Rally’. 1933 Leaving the League In 1933, Hitler pulled Germany out of the League of Nations. He did this after other countries failed to promise disarmament at the League’s conference on the matter. He argued he would continue to re-arm if other countries did. 1934 Dollfuss Affair Dollfuss, the Austrian Chancellor, knew Hitler wanted to unite Germany and Austria so he publicly banned the Nazi party in Austria. Hitler responded by asking the Austrians to revolt and Dollfuss was murdered. However, he didn’t take Austria then as Italy moved to try and stop him and his army wasn’t strong enough. Nevertheless, he knew he had the support of the Austrian people. 1935 Rearmament Hitler held the ‘Freedom to Rearm Rally’ in Germany where he put on a massive display of new weapons and troops. This was a direct violation of the Treaty of Versailles. Hitler's Actions 1935 Hitler continued to be allowed to act in ways that defied the Treaty of Versailles. This encouraged him to continue to break the terms on the assumption that there would be no consequences. 1935 Saar Plebiscite The Saar was a German speaking area given to the League of Nations for 15 years as a part of the Treaty of Versailles. Hitler held a plebiscite (vote) with the people and 90% wanted to go back to Germany. Rearmament funding He marched in and took back the land. He then used its natural resources to further supply his re-armament. 1935 Anglo-German Naval Agreement In reflection of the harshness of the Treaty of Versailles, Britain allowed Hitler to build up his navy to 35% of the British Navy. He was also now allowed submarines. Treaty of Versailles This went directly against the Treaty of Versailles and Hitler thought that this would mean he could continue to break the terms without consequence.

resources.title: The Spanish Civil War, 1936-39

content.topicNotes: The Spanish Civil War, 1936-39: Clash of Ideologies The Spanish Civil War (1936-39) was a key conflict between far-right nationalists and communism, with international powers influencing Spain's future and the start of WWII. Causes and ideologies The Spanish Civil War began in 1936 due to political tensions in Spain. Far-right nationalists, led by General Franco, opposed the Republican communists and socialists. Liberal democracy aimed to preserve a parliamentary system but struggled against dictators. The war reflected the global struggle between fascism and communism. Franco and the Nationalists General Francisco Franco led the Nationalists against the Republicans. Franco promoted far-right nationalists ideas and sought a military dictatorship. The Nationalists received vital support from Italy and Germany. Franco aimed to unify Spain under authoritarian rule. Role of Germany and Italy Germany sent about 16,000 troops and weapons to support Franco. Italy contributed around 70,000 soldiers and strong air power. Hitler and Mussolini wanted to test their military forces before World War II. German and Italian aid gave the Nationalists a significant advantage in the war. The USSR and the Republicans The Soviet Union provided weapons and advisers to the Republican side. The USSR aimed to prevent fascist expansion and spread communism. The Republicans also received help from international brigade volunteers. Despite aid, Republicans lacked the scale of support the Nationalists had. Britain and France Britain and France chose a policy of non-intervention during the conflict. Both feared the war would escalate into a wider European conflict. British and French neutrality limited Republican access to resources and aid. This policy favoured the Nationalist side indirectly. Impact on WWII Franco's victory in 1939 strengthened fascism in Europe. Hitler used Spain as a testing ground for tactics later used in WWII. Franco's win boosted Hitler's confidence in military expansion. The war showed how ideological conflicts foreshadowed global war.

resources.title: The Strengths of North Vietnam 1

content.topicNotes: Geographical and Cultural Strengths of North Vietnam The geographical, cultural, political, economic and military strengths of North Vietnam all contributed to the failure of the USA in Vietnam. Culture The North Vietnamese knew the landscape, culture and language of the South. Tunnels They knew about and could use the tunnel system that had been developed during the war with the French. Family Many North Vietnamese fighters were originally from the South before the 1954 Geneva Accords, and so had family and contacts they could use. Political and Economic Strengths The geographical, cultural, political, economic and military strengths of North Vietnam all contributed to the failure of the USA in Vietnam. Government North Vietnam’s government did not allow any opposition to the War. The VC The VC were already well established in the South, so North Vietnam could work with them and send supplies using the Ho Chi Minh Trail. China and the USSR China and the USSR sent $3billion in aid, weapons and equipment between 1954 and 1967. The Ho Chi Minh Trail Laos and Cambodia allowed the Ho Chi Minh Trail to run through their countries, and there was little the USA could do to stop this without starting more wars. Political and Economic Strengths of North Vietnam North Vietnam’s government did not allow any opposition to the war.

Conditions The North Vietnamese and VC troops were used to fighting in jungle conditions. Tactics They used guerrilla tactics and fought small skirmishes, although they could also fight large battles. Organisation The VC used a system of tunnels and bases to move supplies, troops and equipment. They were well-organised and experienced.

resources.title: The Sudetenland

content.topicNotes: The Sudetenland Chamberlain and Hitler agreed that Germany could have the Sudetenland (in Czechoslovakia) if they promised not to take any more land. The Sudetenland As Hitler and the Nazis grew in power, the British Prime Minister Chamberlain flew to meet Hitler in 1938. They had a conference and decided that Hitler could have the area of the Sudetenland (in Czechoslovakia) if he promised not to take any more land. Appeasement Hitler signed to agree to this and this policy was known as appeasement. Chamberlain thought he had secured ‘peace in our time’. As by giving Hitler land he wanted in Czechoslovakia he would be pleased and not want any more. Avoiding war Chamberlain knew that peace was important to the British people who didn’t want to have another world war. The First World War hadn’t been that long ago and many people remembered the horrors of it. Reasons for Appeasement: Avoiding War Chamberlain knew that peace was important to the British people who didn’t want to have another world war. The First World War hadn’t been that long ago and many people remembered the horrors of it.

resources.title: The Terms: Armaments

content.topicNotes: Armaments After negotiations at the Palace of Versailles, the Treaty of Versailles was drawn up by the Allies. An easy way to remember the TOV is to use the term ‘TRAWL’. A is for Armaments. Aims of disarmament Germany’s armed forces were severely limited to make sure they couldn’t start another war. This clause would also humiliate Germany as previously, they were very proud of their military might under the Kaiser’s leadership. Restrictions They were not allowed an air force. Their army was limited to 100,000 men with no tanks - this was to act as a defensive army only. Their navy was limited to 15,000 men and were only allowed 6 battleships, no submarines, and limited naval ships. Purpose This would mean that Germany’s armed forces could only use their army for defensive purposes if they were attacked and not in an offensive (attacking) war.
content.description: History: Cambridge International GCSE The Twentieth Century (Option B) > Was the Treaty of Versailles Fair? > Did the Victors Get Everything They Wanted?

resources.title: The Terms: Reparations

content.topicNotes: Reparations After negotiations at the Palace of Versailles, the Treaty of Versailles was drawn up by the Allies. An easy way to remember the TOV is to use the term ‘TRAWL’. R is for Reparations. Reparations Reparations means the money Germany had to pay the Allies after WWI to cover damage and losses caused by the war. Germany had to pay a total of 132 billion gold marks to the Allies as compensation for the war. This would take them over 60 years to pay back. In 2010, Germany made its final payment of £59 million, clearing its reparations debt. Poverty These reparations were very costly and Germany would find it very difficult to pay. Germany, like many other countries in Europe, was very poor after the war because wars cost a lot of money. After the war, many people in Germany were so poor that hundreds of thousands died from hunger.
content.description: History: Cambridge International GCSE The Twentieth Century (Option B) > Was the Treaty of Versailles Fair? > Did the Victors Get Everything They Wanted?

resources.title: The Terms: Territory

content.topicNotes: Territory An easy way to remember the TOV is to use the term ‘TRAWL’. T is for Territory: the Germans had lots of land taken off them. Colonies Germany's colonies in Africa were taken away and given to the League of Nations to control as ‘mandates’. In reality, the countries that controlled them were Great Britain and France. The Rhineland The Rhineland - an area of land between France and Germany - was demilitarized. Demilitarization means that no troops or weapons would be allowed there. The reason for this was to create a 'buffer zone' as France feared another German invasion. This was an area that was on the border of Germany. This gave France security that Germany wouldn’t be strong enough militarily to attack them right on their border. The Polish Corridor Germany was split as the Polish Corridor was given to Poland so that they could have access to sea trade. The ‘Polish Corridor’ was an extension of Poland’s territory that cut off East Prussia from the rest of Germany. Poland's emergence was a direct consequence of the Treaty of Versailles. New countries Eight new countries were created in the Treaty of Versailles using land that used to belong to Germany. Due to this, some countries had German-speaking people in them. This would later prove a motivation for Hitler to reunite all German-speaking people. Territory Germans had lots of land taken off them due to the Treaty of Versailles. Confiscated land 13% of all German land was taken away including areas such as:Alsace Lorraine. Eupen. Malmedy. Alsace Lorraine Alsace Lorraine was given to France as it had previously been owned by the country before Germany had taken it in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War. The Saar The Saar (Germany’s industrial area) was given to France to make sure that Germany would pay the reparations to France. If Germany did not pay their reparations, then the Saar would not be returned to them. It would be worth mentioning that the Saar was incredibly economically valuable for Germany as it contained rich coal fields. Then after 15 years, the people would be given the vote whether to return to Germany or not. Anschluss Germany had united with Austria in an alliance during the First World War. One of the terms of the Treaty was that Germany wasn’t allowed to ever unite with Austria (Anschluss) again. The term Anschluss means unification with Austria. German citizens After the creation of new countries and the removal of German land, a total of 6 million German people were no longer living on German soil. In total, 13% of all German land was taken away.

resources.title: The Terms: War Guilt

content.topicNotes: War Guilt and the League of Nations After negotiations at the Palace of Versailles, the Treaty of Versailles was drawn up by the Allies. An easy way to remember the TOV is to use the term ‘TRAWL’. W is for War Guilt and L is for the League of Nations. War Guilt Under Article 231 of the Treaty, the Germans had to accept full responsibility for causing the First World War. This was known as the war guilt clause. Humiliation This was very humiliating for the Germans and they believed that they hadn’t caused the war. They were also humiliated in front of the whole world and were seen as an outcast. League of Nations This was set up after the war to promote peace and co-operation between countries of the world. Germany was not allowed to join the League because they were seen as the instigators of WW1. Germany was therefore viewed as a threat to international peace. This did little to show the German people that they were still internationally recognised as a powerful and peaceful country. They seemed an outcast. The War Guilt Clause This was very humiliating for the Germans and they believed that they hadn’t caused the war. They were also humiliated in front of the whole world and were seen as an outcast. The League of Nations Set up after the war to promote peace and co-operation between countries of the world. Peace Co-operation

resources.title: The Tet Offensive, 1968

content.topicNotes: The Tet Offensive, 1968 The North and VC launched a surprise attack on 26 cities in South during the 1968 New Year’s Tet festival. Surprise attack The North and VC launched a surprise attack on 26 cities in South during the 1968 New Year’s Tet festival. The VC pretended to want peace talks as a decoy. Meanwhile, they attacked near the demilitarised zone. This was to draw US troops away from the cities. Saigon and Hue 84,000 communist troops then attacked southern cities on 30th January. When there was the Tet ceasefire. Most famously, the city of Hue was captured. And the US embassy in Saigon was taken for 6 hours. The attack in Saigon was beaten by US troops in 2 days, and within 3 weeks in Hue. US shock It shocked people in the US as they had been told they were winning the war. But as it was all reported on TV people saw that they weren’t. The South didn’t rise up in revolution like the VC had expected. And the VC were nearly wiped out in the fighting. The VC’s only victory The communists lost 45,000 men. Although they couldn’t win by direct attack, they showed that they could launch a huge surprise attack on the US. The VC’s only lasting victory was that they could use it in propaganda. Anti-war protests The Tet Offensive led to huge anti-war protests in America with over 150,000 people. It led to peace talks in 1968 which were a turning point in the war. The Role of the Media The Tet Offensive shocked people in the US as they had been told they were winning the war, but as it was all reported on TV people saw that perhaps they weren’t.

resources.title: The Treaty of Versailles

content.topicNotes: The Paris Peace Conference 27 countries met at the Palace of Versailles (France) in 1919. They were made up of the victorious allies. The end of the war By spring 1918 the leaders of Germany’s army realised it was no longer possible to win the war. Germany was suffering from major food shortages. As a result, the military told the government to stop. Having lost support of the Germany army, Kaiser Wilhelm stepped down on 9 November 1918. The Palace of Versailles 32 countries met at the Palace of Versailles (France) in 1919. They were made up of the victorious allies. Britain, France, and the USA Germany was not present at this conference because they were not invited. They met to decide how to deal with the losing countries. The Conference One of their aims was to prevent another war from happening again. Out of all of the countries that attended, there were 3 leaders who were the most powerful and influential. These were the leaders of France, America and Great Britain. They were known as the ‘Big Three’. The conference lasted 12 months. The Treaty of Versailles (TOV) After negotiations at the Palace of Versailles, the Treaty of Versailles was drawn up by the Allies. The Treaty After negotiations at the Palace of Versailles, the Treaty of Versailles was drawn up by the Allies. The Treaty aimed at weakening Germany financially, economically and socially so that another war launched by Germany would seem impossible. Terms The Germans were given no time to negotiate. They had to accept the terms as set out in the Treaty. The Germans were told they had to sign the treaty or the allies would resume the war. Which would almost certainly result in Germany being invaded and taken over by the allies. The Treaty of Versailles The Germans were given no time to negotiate. They had to accept the terms as set out in the Treaty. The Germans were given only the choice to sign the treaty or if not the Allies would resume the war.

resources.title: The Truman Doctrine & Marshall Plan

content.topicNotes: The Truman Doctrine The Truman Doctrine describes a speech given by the US President, Harry Truman. In the speech, he committed to intervening to help to spread capitalism and limit the spread of communism. This was a policy called ‘containment’. The 'domino effect' In 1947, Truman gave his speech urging communism to be contained. At this time, communist parties (supported by the USSR) were already in control of Poland, Romania and Bulgaria. President Truman was scared that other countries in Eastern Europe and the Middle East would fall to Communism. Truman was scared of something called a ‘domino effect’. As more nations got communist governments, they would then support communist revolutions in nearby countries funding populist uprisings. Winston Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech Winston Churchill, no longer Prime Minister of the UK, gave a significant speech in March 1946 in Fulton, USA. He argued that ‘an iron curtain has descended across the continent of Europe’. This iron curtain speech described the USSR's behaviour in Eastern Europe. By this, Churchill meant that Europe was now divided — a communist east under Soviet influence and a capitalist west supported by the USA. The Truman Doctrine The exact contents of the Truman Doctrine said: "I believe that it must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures. I believe that we must assist free peoples to work out their own destinies in their own way." He committed to giving political, military and financial aid to countries to stop the spread of communism. The Domino Effect In 1947, Poland, Romania and Bulgaria already had communist governments. Truman feared this may spread to other countries. He feared a ‘domino effect'. The Marshall Plan (Marshall Aid) The Marshall Plan (also known as Marshall Aid) formalised the economic assistance that Truman described in the Truman Doctrine of 1947. The Marshall Plan of 1947 The Marshall Plan provided economic assistance to back up the Truman Doctrine. It was named after George Marshall, the US Secretary of State at the time. The money was spent to encourage trade with the United States, and a Technical Assistance Program was designed to implement improvements aimed at increasing productivity. Josef Stalin stopped any communist nations supported by the Soviet Union from accepting Marshall Aid. 'Containment' Through the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan, the USA sought to contain communism through military and economic assistance to primarily Western European countries. This was part of a policy known as ‘containment’. The Truman Doctrine and the 1947 Marshall Plan increased tensions between the Soviets and the US. Soviet perspective on the Marshall Plan The Soviet Union saw both the 1947 Truman Doctrine and the 1947 Marshall Plan as a threat to Eastern Europe. The Soviet Politburo (leadership board of the communist party in Russia) viewed the Marshall Plan as an example of America's 'economic imperialism'. US perspective on the Marshall Plan In the US, the Marshall Plan was a highly successful foreign policy initiative for promoting economic recovery and political stability in Western Europe. The US perspective Politicians argued that the Soviets were trying to isolate Eastern Europe from the West by installing communist governments and banning them from accepting aid. In reality, given the fact that most of the aid went to Britain and France, this view is challenged. Truman's beliefs The USA believed that rebuilding the economies of war-damaged countries would make communism less appealing. Truman thought that if people had stable jobs and prosperity, they would be less likely to support communist ideas, which required giving up private wealth and property to the state. Increasing Tensions Europe became the ideological battleground between the two emerging superpowers, the USA and the USSR. The Marshall Plan and Truman Doctrine (in 1947) raised tensions. Tense Tense

resources.title: The U2 Crisis

content.topicNotes: The U2 Crisis In early May 1960 the Soviet Union shot down an American U2 spy plane. The Paris Peace Conference At the Paris Peace Conference in May 1960, talks between the USA and USSR broke down as the Soviet Union shot down an American U2 spy plane. The US claimed that it was a weather plane, but the Soviets captured the pilot, Gary Powers. A lack of resolution Khrushchev wanted President Eisenhower to apologise but the US President did not. The peace conference ended, but tensions between the two countries increased. Cuban Missile Crisis The increased tensions were reflected by the Cuban Missile Crisis a few years later and by the fact that there were no meaningful official agreements on the arms race between the two nations for 10 more years. The Cuban Missile Crisis The increased tensions were reflected by the Cuban Missile Crisis a few years later and by the fact that there were no meaningful official agreements on the arms race between the two nations for 10 more years. U2 In early May 1960 the Soviet Union shot down an American U2 spy plane. This ended the talks at the Paris Peace Conference. U2 Spy Plane U2

resources.title: The US and Korea: Background to the Crisis

content.topicNotes: The US and Korea: Background to the Crisis The US faced communist expansions in Europe and Asia during Truman's presidency, leading to military and political actions that set the stage for the Korean conflict. Truman and containment policy President Truman led the US to stop communism's spread after World War II. Truman introduced the policy of containment in 1947 to prevent Soviet expansion. Truman's program of massive rearmament increased US military strength significantly. The US committed to defend countries threatened by communism worldwide. Communism in Czechoslovakia Communists took control in Czechoslovakia in 1948, alarming the US. The US saw Czechoslovakia's fall as Soviet aggression in Eastern Europe. Truman increased support to Western Europe to prevent more communist takeovers. This event reinforced US efforts to contain Soviet influence. The Berlin Blockade (1948-1949) The USSR blocked all land routes to West Berlin in 1948. Truman organized the Berlin Airlift to supply West Berlin with food and fuel. The airlift showed US resolve to oppose Soviet pressure without war. The USSR ended the blockade in 1949, marking a Cold War victory for the US. China's Communist Revolution Communist forces led by Mao Zedong seized control of China in 1949. The US had supported the Nationalists but failed to prevent communist victory. China's shift alarmed Truman and strengthened the communist bloc in Asia. This event increased US urgency to confront communist expansion in Korea. USSR's nuclear weapons The USSR tested its first atomic bomb in 1949, ending US nuclear monopoly. Truman's government accelerated nuclear weapons development in response. The nuclear threat intensified Cold War tensions and arms race dynamics. US policies became more aggressive to counter Soviet military power. Prelude to the Korean crisis Truman's policies aimed to defend South Korea from communist North Korean invasion. The US provided military and economic aid to South Korea before 1950. The combined fear of Soviet and Chinese support for communism influenced US actions. These events led directly to US involvement in the Korean War starting in 1950.

resources.title: The USSR & Eastern Europe

content.topicNotes: The USSR and Eastern Europe In the aftermath of WW2, communism swept across Eastern Europe. Spread of communism In reaction to fascism and the devastation caused by war, left-wing politics gained more traction in Eastern Europe. Many people were disillusioned with pre-war governments and blamed capitalism for unemployment and inequality. Communist parties also promised jobs, equality, and stability at a time of widespread economic hardship. Sphere of influence At the Yalta Conference, the Allies discussed how to manage post-war Europe. The term ‘sphere of influence’ refers to an area where one country has strong political, military, or economic control over others. Yalta is considered the first clear expression of a Soviet 'sphere of influence' because Stalin was allowed to have more influence in Eastern Europe, while the USA and Britain focused on Western Europe. Controlling elections At Yalta, Stalin agreed to the Declaration of Liberated Europe, which stated that countries liberated from Nazi control after the war could hold free elections to choose their governments. Communist Parties came to power under the pretence of democracy. In reality, opposition leaders were intimidated or removed, and most countries in Eastern Europe did not have genuinely free elections. Communist states By 1949, the Soviet Union’s satellite states included Bulgaria, Romania, Poland, Hungary and Czechoslovakia. The Soviet Union viewed these states as a buffer to the west (as hostilities with the US were escalating) and an opportunity to spread communism. Free Elections in Eastern Europe Communist Parties came to power under the pretence of democracy. In reality, most countries in Eastern Europe did not have free elections. USSR Control over Eastern Europe After 1945 The USSR established control over Eastern Europe from 1945, using political manipulation, coalitions, and purges in countries like Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria, and Yugoslavia. Czechoslovakia The USSR supported Benes but allowed communist influence to grow. The Czech Communist Party won many votes in the 1946 election. Communists pressured non-communists to lose power by 1948. The 1948 election saw communist domination and the end of democracy. Hungary's shift to communism Hungary held free elections in 1945, winning mostly non-communists. The secret police controlled by communists suppressed opposition. The USSR helped rig the 1947 election to favour communists. By 1948, Hungary was a communist state under Soviet control. Poland's communist takeover The USSR formed the Lublin government dominated by communists in 1945. Poland held elections in 1947, manipulated by Soviet-backed communists. The coalition government had no real power against the Communist Party. Opposition politicians were removed or silenced by 1947. Romania under Soviet influence Romania's Communist Party gained control after 1945 coalitions. The USSR demanded reparations from Romania for war damage. The 1946 elections were falsified to secure communist victory. King Michael was forced to abdicate after show trials against opponents. Bulgaria and Yugoslavia's paths Bulgaria had a communist coalition by 1945, purging the opposition. Bulgaria ended its monarchy and created a communist constitution. Yugoslavia, led by Broz, formed the Popular Front and declared a republic. Yugoslavia acted independently, resisting Stalin's full control. Iran and Turkey The USSR occupied northern Iran but withdrew due to US and UN pressure. Turkey allowed the USSR to build a naval base on the Dardanelles. The USA opposed Soviet presence in Turkey threatening security. Stalin withdrew Soviet forces from Turkey under international pressure.

resources.title: The Vietcong

content.topicNotes: The Increasing Threat of the Vietcong The ARVN were too busy arguing about who should be the leader rather than working to defeat the VC, despite having five times more troops. Johnson's aims After Kennedy’s assassination, Johnson became President. Johnson wanted to continue Kennedy’s goal of supporting a democratic South Vietnam. Johnson also wanted to stop communism from spreading. At the same time, Johnson hoped to avoid a larger war involving the USA. Problems The ARVN had five times more troops than the Viet Cong. But the ARVN were more focused on leadership struggles than fighting. This made it harder to defeat the VC. On the other hand, the NLF were very well organised. The NLF used small, fast-moving cells of Viet Cong fighters. Support China sent $100 million in aid to South Vietnam, using the Ho Chi Minh trail. The Southern government was still unpopular as it was seen as a puppet of the USA. The VC The VC gained local support by introducing reforms and using propaganda. The VC began to attack more often and attacked more US military targets. Johnson increased the number of advisors in South Vietnam to 200,000. Aims of the USA After Kennedy’s assassination, President Johnson wanted to continue his aims of ensuring South Vietnam had a democratic, popular government that would oppose communism, and avoid the USA getting involved in an escalating war.

resources.title: The Weaknesses of the US 1

content.topicNotes: Geographical and Cultural Weaknesses The US were at a huge disadvantage in the Vietnam War, due to geographical, cultural, political, economic and military reasons, which all came together to cause their failure. Racism Americans were foreigners fighting in a strange country, and many had racist attitudes towards the Vietnamese. Language They had to use interpreters as they didn’t speak the language, which made it harder to gain support from the locals. Cultural customs Most Americans had no idea about the customs and culture of Vietnam and didn’t understand that Vietnamese villagers didn’t want to leave their land where their ancestors were buried. Literacy They didn’t realise that most Vietnamese villagers couldn’t read, so dropping leaflets warning them to move out before bombing raids didn’t work. American Cultural Insensitivity Most Americans had no idea what the country was like, and didn’t understand that villagers didn’t want to leave their land where their ancestors were buried. Political and Economic Weaknesses The US were at a huge disadvantage in the Vietnam War, due to geographical, cultural, political, economic and military reasons, which all came together to cause their failure. Distrust of motives Many South Vietnamese viewed the USA as a foreign occupier imposing ideas, like the French before them. They did not believe the US was fighting for democracy, despite its claims. Corruption The US backed South Vietnamese government was corrupt. Many officials had worked for the French, making them even more unpopular. Home opposition The USA faced opposition at home, both in the form of anti-war protests and restricted funding from Congress after 1971.
content.description: History: Cambridge International GCSE The Twentieth Century (Option B) > Did the US Contain the Spread of Communism? > The US and Vietnam, 1955-75

resources.title: The Weaknesses of the US 2

content.topicNotes: Military Weaknesses The US were at a huge disadvantage in the Vietnam War, due to geographical, cultural, political, economic and military reasons, which all came together to cause their failure. Limitations The military believed that the war could be won if they were given more troops and bombing campaigns in North Vietnam, not by fighting the limited war the government wanted. Resentment They ignored the fact that the South Vietnamese government didn’t control large parts of the South. They also ignored that burning villages caused resentment, instead focusing on the number of VC troops killed or bases destroyed. Work on gaining the support of the villagers was inconsistent. Inexperience The draft meant many US soldiers were young and inexperienced. Drafted soldiers only stayed in Vietnam for a year before returning home, meaning the most experienced soldiers left. Lack of training Soldiers’ morale dropped due to the lack of training in how to fight against guerrilla tactics. Fragging Soldiers tried to avoid combat and ‘fragging’ and drug abuse became a big problem.

resources.title: US & Soviet Attitudes to Peace

content.topicNotes: US & Soviet Attitudes to Peace Stalin sought security via Eastern Europe control. The US aimed to stop communism through containment. Roosevelt promoted democracy; Truman used the atomic bomb, sparking Cold War tensions. Stalin's foreign policy goals Stalin focused on Soviet security after WWII. Stalin wanted to create a buffer zone in Eastern Europe to prevent future invasions. Stalin aimed to spread Soviet influence through communist governments. Stalin's policy showed a desire for control, not peace with the West. Reasons for Soviet actions Stalin remembered the invasions from Germany in WWI and WWII. Stalin feared another invasion would destroy the Soviet Union. Stalin used Soviet armies to establish friendly governments in Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia. Stalin believed this influence stopped the West from attacking again. WWII consequences for the USSR The USSR suffered around 27 million deaths in WWII. The war destroyed 1,700 towns and 70,000 villages in the Soviet Union. The Soviet farms lost 25 million horses and 30 million cattle. The USSR faced millions of refugees and major economic damage. Roosevelt's attitude to empires Roosevelt supported the idea of self-determination for all nations. Roosevelt opposed large empires and 'spheres of influence.' Roosevelt promoted democracy and cooperation after the war. Roosevelt believed peace depended on freedom and international cooperation. US policy on containment The US wanted to stop the spread of communism worldwide. The US used containment to limit Soviet influence in Europe and Asia. The US supported countries threatened by communism with money and military aid. The US aimed to protect democracy and capitalism globally. Truman and the atomic bomb Truman became US President in April 1945 after Roosevelt died. Truman used the atomic bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Truman aimed to end WWII quickly and show US power to the USSR. Truman's use of the bomb increased tensions and started the Cold War.
content.description: History: Cambridge International GCSE The Twentieth Century (Option B) > Who was to Blame for the Cold War? > Why did the US-Soviet Alliance Break Down?

resources.title: US Tactics

content.topicNotes: US Tactics The US focused on winning the war through capturing land and killing the VC, rather than gaining public support. Operation Rolling Thunder Johnson wanted to bomb North Vietnam into surrender, rather than sending US troops to Vietnam. It targeted the Ho Chi Minh trail and industry, but not the capital Hanoi and not the port where Soviet supplies arrived in the North. 90,000 were killed, and it cost the US $4billion. Failures of Operation Rolling Thunder However it failed because the VC used tunnels under the Ho Chi Minh trail to avoid the bombings, so supplies continued. The USSR and China sent military supplies into the North, so the destruction of industry didn’t matter too much. The USSR sent $505 million in aid in 1967. Also, the high civilian death rates made the USA even more unpopular. Napalm As well as conventional bombs, Operation Rolling Thunder used napalm. A highly flammable substance made from petrol thickened with soaps that stuck to skin and burnt through to the bone. Pineapple bombs They also used pineapple bombs that sprayed pellets everywhere when they exploded, shooting into people like bullets. US Tactics The US focused on winning the war through capturing land and killing the VC, rather than gaining public support. Search and Destroy In March 1965, 3500 US marines arrived in South Vietnam. Small units of them (supported by the ARVN) would hunt down and destroy VC villages in the South by bombing or using chemical weapons. Operation Cedar Falls One example was Operation Cedar Falls in 1967 where the US burnt down villages for three weeks, killing 750 VC. Despite some early successes in finding and killing VC fighters, as soon as the US troops left the VC returned to the area. The attacks made 4 million South Vietnamese into refugees from the violence, making the US and South Vietnamese government even more unpopular. Agent Orange Agent Orange was a weedkiller used to destroy jungle and farmland. It helped the US find VC bases and stop villagers from feeding the Viet Cong. From 1964 to 1971, Operation Ranch Hand sprayed chemicals across South Vietnam. Over 24% of the land and 3,000 villages were affected. It poisoned water supplies and caused serious health problems, sometimes fatal.
content.description: History: Cambridge International GCSE The Twentieth Century (Option B) > Did the US Contain the Spread of Communism? > The US and Vietnam, 1955-75

resources.title: Vietcong Tactics

content.topicNotes: Vietcong Tactics Guerrilla warfare, the Ho Chi Minh Trail, tunnels and booby traps were the main Vietcong tactics. Guerrilla warfare Guerrilla warfare is when fighters avoid open battles and instead ambush their enemies. It was used due to small size of VC compared to USA. It was hard for the ARVN and USA to fight back because the VC blended into villages as they wore no uniform. Ambush attacks, infiltrated US army bases/cities and laid traps. Ho Chi Minh Trail A 600-mile trail through Laos and Cambodia used to provide supplies from North/China for attacks in South. The USA couldn’t stop it as goes through other countries, and they wouldn’t declare war on them. Tunnels The VC used tunnels as bases and ambush spots. They contained hospitals, storage and weapons and allowed the VC to move unseen across 400km of South Vietnam. The US couldn’t fit in the tunnels to destroy them, so simply destroyed any entrances they found. Booby Traps Examples of VC traps would be Punji sticks covered in excrement or Bouncing Betty mines laid by women and children. 19% of US casualties were caused by traps.

resources.title: Vietnamisation

content.topicNotes: Vietnamisation President Nixon won the election in 1969 as he promised to end the war in Vietnam, but ensure it wouldn’t fall to the communists. He tried several different methods: Official peace talks Official peace talks: Nixon sent representatives to negotiate with North and South Vietnam, as well as the VC. However, this would be a very long and difficult process. Secret peace talks Secret peace talks:Nixon sent Henry Kissinger to negotiate secretly with the leader of North Vietnam, Le Duc Tho. Troop withdrawal Troop withdrawal: Nixon decreased the number of troops in Vietnam by 25,000 and began to withdraw them from July 1969 onwards. ARVN training ARVN training: Nixon ordered General Abrams to focus on training the ARVN to carry on the war without American troops. Secret bombings Secret bombings: In March 1969 Nixon ordered bombs to be dropped on the Ho Chi Minh trail in Cambodia. The Nixon Doctrine On 25th July 1969 Nixon made a speech about the role of the USA in the future of South East Asia. This became known as Vietnamisation. Vietnamisation On 25th July 1969 Nixon made a speech about the role of the USA in the future of South East Asia. This became known as Vietnamisation. Nixon's speech The USA promised to support its allies against nuclear threats by training their troops, but without sending US soldiers. This was like in 1964, when the US gave advice and money but kept its soldiers out. 'Withdraw with honour’ Vietnamisation would allow the US to ‘withdraw with honour’ in the eyes of the Nixon administration. And South Vietnam would remain an independent, non-communist country. Divisions The US public welcomed Vietnamisation. But the army leadership felt that the US was withdrawing before the ARVN were ready. And that after the Tet Offensive, more troops would give them a chance to fully defeat the VC. 'Withdraw With Honour’ Vietnamisation would allow the US to ‘withdraw with honour’ and that South Vietnam would remain an independent, non-communist country.

resources.title: WWII & Failure of the League of Nations

content.topicNotes: The Start of WWII Very few people believed Hitler would stay truthful to the Munich Agreement and concern started to quickly build. Hitler then made some decisions that eventually forced the Allies to declare war. Invasion of Czechoslovakia Czechoslovakia began to unravel as soon as the Sudetenland had been conceded. In March 1939, the Czechoslovakian president was persuaded by Hitler to let German troops enter the country as a last resort to try and 'restore order'. There was no immediate reaction from France and Britain despite Hitler having clearly broken his side of the deal. The 'Pact of Steel' This pact was signed by Germany and Italy in May 1939. This pact stated that these countries would support one another if war broke out. The Nazi-Soviet Pact Despite not trusting the Nazis, Stalin (the Soviet leader) negotiated with them after the Munich Conference. In August 1939, the USSR and Germany formally agreed to not attack one another by signing the Nazi-Soviet Pact. This pact also included secret plans to divide Poland up between them. Invasion of Poland The Nazis invaded Poland on the 1st of September, 1939. Hitler was ordered to leave by France and Britain. When Hitler refused, Britain declared war. This happened on the 3rd of September, 1939. Why Did the League of Nations Fail? The original aims of keeping peace and promoting international cooperation were not achieved by the League of Nations. Its influence began to decrease after its major failures and eventually fell apart in 1946. Was the League always bound to fail? The refusal of the USA to join put Britain and France in a difficult position. Britain and France were overstretched in trying to financially and militarily support the League by themselves. The Treaty of Versailles established the League. And so had to defend the unpopular Treaty. Failing of the League By not initially letting Germany or Russia sign, the League excluded two nations that were capable of big contributions. The League's ineffective and slow decision-making was a by-product of its clumsy organisational structure. Bad decisions The League lacked the strength to counter aggressive moves. The League failed to appropriately deal with ambitious members. The Covenant was abused by lots of members. Who decided to leave when challenged about their violations. The League allowed alliances to sneak back into play in place of cooperation. As soon as faith in the League began to diminish, countries boosted their military capacity in expectation of another war. Control The global political situation became much more tense because of The Great Depression of the 1930s. The weakening of the economies of League members made them less capable of responding to international threats. As they were preoccupied with dealing with issues closer to home. There is also the argument that stopping Hitler and Mussolini was a task too great for any organisation. Members and Non-Members of the League of Nations USA The USA chose not to join the League. Germany Germany was one of two powerful nations who were initially forbidden from joining the League. Russia Russia was one of two powerful nations who were initially forbidden from joining the League. Britain Along with France, Britain was largely responsible for financially and militarily supporting the League. France Along with Britain, France was largely responsible for financially and militarily supporting the League.

resources.title: Åland Islands 1920-21

content.topicNotes: The Åland Islands Dispute 1920-21 The League of Nations resolved the Åland Islands dispute in 1920-21. Background The Åland Islands lie between Sweden and Finland in the Baltic Sea. The Åland population spoke Swedish and wished to join Sweden. Finland controlled the islands after independence in 1917. Finland wanted to keep them because they were new and didn’t want to lose territory. The Åland Islands location would help Finland move their navy around and protect their trade routes. Sweden supported the islanders' demand to unite with Sweden. The Åland crisis Sweden and Finland argued over Åland's sovereignty in 1919. The islanders appealed for help from the League of Nations in 1920. The League saw the dispute as a test for its role in peacekeeping. The League hoped to avoid war between Sweden and Finland. League of Nations' role The League created a commission to investigate the Åland dispute. The commission visited the islands and consulted both countries. The League recommended that Finland keep sovereignty over Åland. The League demanded Finland guarantee the islands' autonomy and demilitarisation. Outcome of the Åland decision The League announced its decision in June 1921. Finland accepted League control of Åland's autonomy conditions. Sweden accepted the League's decision but expressed disappointment. The islanders remained Swedish-speaking but under Finnish rule. Failures of the League The League's decision did not satisfy all parties involved. The League failed to prevent tensions between Finland and Sweden. The Åland dispute exposed the League's limited influence in peacekeeping. Significance The Åland case showed the League could mediate peacefully. The League's ruling preserved regional peace for many years. The Åland experience shaped future peacekeeping efforts by the League.

Indicative content:
- Appeasement can be seen as naïve because some historians argue that British politicians placed too much trust in Hitler, who had already stated in 'My Struggle' that he would gladly take up arms, meaning giving in to his demands simply encouraged him to ask for more.
- Politicians such as Churchill argued that repeatedly saying 'yes' to Hitler made Britain look weak, and that refusing to stand firm gave Hitler no reason to stop his aggression, effectively rewarding his behaviour.
- Appeasement had a wider dangerous effect beyond Germany, as other powerful dictators including Stalin of the USSR, Mussolini of Italy, and Japan observed that Hitler faced no consequences, giving them the idea that they too could act as they pleased.
- There were reasons to justify appeasement, as many felt the Treaty of Versailles had been too harsh on Germany and that some of Hitler's early demands were understandable corrections of an unjust peace, making concessions appear reasonable rather than naïve.

Indicative content:
- Appeasement was justified because both Britain and France had not re-armed and needed more time to prepare for a possible war, meaning that making concessions to Hitler bought valuable time to build up their military strength.
- The memory of the Treaty of Versailles gave appeasement moral justification: many in Britain believed the treaty had been too punitive on Germany, so allowing Hitler to revise it seemed reasonable rather than simply weak.
- Appeasement ultimately failed because Hitler broke his promises almost immediately; following the Munich Agreement of 1938, in which Hitler pledged not to invade any more of Czechoslovakia, he invaded the rest of the country just months later, showing concessions did not satisfy his ambitions.
- The policy of appeasement allowed Hitler to grow stronger unchecked; Britain and France failed to act when he remilitarised the Rhineland and when Germany carried out the Anschluss with Austria, both direct violations of the Treaty of Versailles, emboldening further aggression.

Indicative content:
- Chamberlain genuinely believed that appeasement had secured 'peace in our time', and by agreeing at the 1938 conference to give Hitler the Sudetenland in exchange for a promise of no further territorial demands, he avoided an immediate outbreak of war between Britain and Germany.
- The British public strongly did not want another world war; memories of the First World War were fresh, and Chamberlain's policy of appeasement reflected the genuine desire of the people he represented to avoid repeating those horrors.
- Hitler broke his promise almost immediately, going on to seize more territory beyond the Sudetenland, which showed that appeasement had failed to stop German aggression and may have encouraged Hitler to believe Britain would not resist further expansion.
- By handing over the Sudetenland — part of Czechoslovakia — without consulting the Czechoslovak government, Chamberlain sacrificed a sovereign nation's territory, undermining trust in Britain as a reliable ally and weakening collective resistance to Nazi expansionism.

Indicative content:
- Comecon, founded in 1949, extended Soviet influence by providing financial aid and encouraging trade with the USSR, drawing in satellite states including Bulgaria, Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Romania, and East Germany, binding them economically to Moscow.
- Comecon banned any member nation from accepting Marshall Plan money from the Americans, meaning it directly cut off Soviet satellite states from Western economic influence, cementing their dependence on the USSR.
- Cominform, founded in 1947, extended Soviet influence by actively encouraging communist uprisings across Europe, supporting parties such as the Revolutionary Communist Party in Great Britain and working to spread communist ideology beyond the existing satellite states.
- Cominform also worked to destroy communist opposition within the USSR's satellite states in Eastern Europe, consolidating Soviet political control, with historian Mark Pittaway noting that USSR-backed communists used rigged elections — such as those in Yugoslavia and Albania in 1945 where communists achieved 93% of the vote — to entrench their rule.

- Brezhnev and Erich Honecker feared that the Prague Spring would inspire calls for similar reforms elsewhere in the Soviet Union's sphere of influence, making the spread of reform a key motivation for intervention.

Indicative content:
- France did achieve some of its goals at the Paris Peace Conference; Germany was forced to pay reparations and its military was limited in size, reflecting France's desire to punish Germany for the damage and casualties it had suffered.
- Germany was weakened by the Treaty of Versailles, which aligned with France's core aim of reducing the threat of a future German attack on French soil, suggesting France achieved at least part of what it sought.
- However, France did not achieve complete demilitarisation of Germany; even Clemenceau had wanted Germany to have no army at all, yet the treaty only limited the army rather than abolishing it, meaning France fell short of its most extreme demands.
- French people widely believed the reparations were set too low and that Germany should have been made to pay far more; since the reparations figure did not satisfy French opinion, France cannot be said to have fully achieved its goals on this issue.
- The disagreements among the Big Three — France, Britain, and the USA — meant that Clemenceau had to compromise, as Britain wanted Germany strong enough to trade with and the USA opposed harsh punishment, limiting how much France could impose its preferred terms.

- Clemenceau's demand for strict German disarmament and security guarantees for France ensured the treaty's punitive character, which critics argued made a future conflict more, rather than less, likely.

Indicative content:
- Germany's failure to pay reparation instalments in 1922 directly triggered the crisis, as it gave France and Belgium justification under the Treaty of Versailles to seize the Ruhr in 1923, taking Germany's most important industrial region.
- The reparations burden of 132 billion gold marks, combined with war debts that amounted to 175% of Germany's total national output, placed enormous financial strain on the Weimar Republic from the outset, making default almost inevitable.
- The seizure of the Ruhr itself was a major cause of the crisis, as France and Belgium took control of all factories, mines and railways in the region, devastating German industrial output regardless of the reparations question.
- The German government's own decision to print more money after the Ruhr crisis, in order to fund passive resistance and pay the Allies more quickly, directly caused hyperinflation, meaning government policy — not reparations alone — drove the worst economic consequences of 1923.

Indicative content:

This removed the threat of Soviet military intervention and encouraged protesters in East Germany to push for democratic change without fear of suppression.
- Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika inspired demands for civil liberties across Soviet satellite states. At the 7th October 1989 parade in East Germany, representatives from twenty-eight regions were openly calling for democratic reforms, showing how Soviet reform policies had directly fuelled the protests that led to the wall's collapse.
- The immediate trigger for the Berlin Wall falling on 9th November 1989 was a mistake by an East German government official, who incorrectly announced the opening of checkpoints at a press conference. Border guards, given no clear instructions, eventually let crowds through, meaning the wall's fall was the result of an unplanned error rather than a deliberate consequence of ending the Brezhnev Doctrine.
- The stubbornness of the East German leadership also played a significant role. Gorbachev himself stated in 2009 that if the East German leader had not been so resistant to change and had introduced his own perestroika, the internal struggle that produced the mass protests outside the Stasi headquarters in Leipzig throughout the summer of 1989 might have been avoided.

- Hitler had believed that Britain and France would back down and not honour their commitments to Poland, as they had done previously. - Furthermore, Hitler had secured his eastern flank through the Nazi-Soviet Pact before the invasion, meaning the Soviet Union would not immediately oppose him. The signing of the Pact of Steel in 1939 also gave Germany the formal military alliance of Italy, suggesting Hitler had made significant diplomatic preparations before launching the attack.

- The risk was also reduced by the fact that the Allies had little desire to go to war over the Rhineland, feeling that Hitler was simply reclaiming land that was German in the first place, and were also preoccupied with their own domestic problems, making Allied inaction highly likely.

- The Saar Plebiscite of 1935 represented a further challenge, as Hitler used the vote — in which 90% of the population chose to return to Germany — to reclaim Saar territory that had been placed under League of Nations control, and then exploited its natural resources to fund further rearmament.

Indicative content:

- People on fixed incomes, including the elderly relying on fixed pensions, and small business owners, were particularly devastated, as they could neither renegotiate their earnings nor recover the savings they had lost once hyperinflation ended.
- However, some groups benefited from hyperinflation: people with debts found it easier to pay them off as the real value of what they owed fell sharply, meaning hyperinflation effectively wiped out their financial obligations.
- Farmers also gained from hyperinflation because consumers paid ever-higher prices for food, increasing farmers' incomes at a time when most other groups were suffering, showing that the impact of the crisis was not uniform across German society.

When the Paris Peace Conference failed to deliver lands such as Dalmatia and Fiume, Italian delegates protested loudly, describing the outcome as a 'mutilated victory'.

- China also suffered a major injustice at Versailles in 1919: it had hoped to regain Shandong Province from Germany, but the treaty instead handed control to Japan without China's consent. China's humiliation was arguably just as acute, and it triggered significant nationalist movements within the country.
- Japan was denied its proposed race equality clause in the League of Nations Covenant by leading powers including Britain and the USA. This rejection wounded Japan's sense of its standing as a world power and contributed to its dissatisfaction with the post-war settlement, ultimately fuelling aggressive expansion in the 1930s.

Indicative content:

- The admission of West Germany (Federal Republic of Germany) into NATO in 1955 deepened the division, as it signalled the permanent military integration of a rearmed Germany into the Western bloc, making reunification and reconciliation with the East far less likely.
- NATO was itself partly a response to earlier Soviet actions, such as the Berlin Blockade (1948–1949) and the communist takeover of Eastern Europe, suggesting the division of Europe had begun before NATO was founded and NATO was a consequence rather than the main cause.
- The formation of the Warsaw Pact in 1955 was the Soviet Union's direct response to NATO, and it was this Soviet decision to bind Eastern European nations into a rival military alliance that institutionalised and entrenched the division of Europe into two opposing blocs.

- The bombing campaign was undermined because the Viet Cong used tunnels under the Ho Chi Minh trail to avoid destruction, meaning supplies continued to flow south despite the bombardment, making the strategy fundamentally flawed.
- However, Search and Destroy missions such as Operation Cedar Falls in 1967 also contributed to failure, as they turned 4 million South Vietnamese into refugees, deepening opposition to the US and the South Vietnamese government rather than securing support.
- External factors also limited US success: the USSR sent $505 million in aid to North Vietnam in 1967 and both the USSR and China continued supplying military equipment, meaning the destruction of North Vietnamese industry through bombing had limited overall effect.

Indicative content:
- Historians such as John Lewis Gaddis developed the post-revisionist school of thought from the 1970s, which blended elements of both the orthodox and revisionist interpretations, meaning responsibility for the Cold War was shared between both superpowers rather than placed solely on one side.
- The post-revisionist approach reflected a broader trend in academic history during this period towards more balanced and nuanced analysis, suggesting the even-handedness was part of a wider scholarly shift rather than unique to Cold War historiography.
- The earlier orthodox interpretation had placed almost all blame on the Soviet Union, while the revisionist school blamed the United States, meaning both preceding schools were themselves one-sided, which makes the post-revisionist position comparatively more balanced but does not make it perfectly neutral.
- From 1989 onwards, the opening of Soviet archives in Moscow and the fall of the communist regime led historians, including John Lewis Gaddis, to shift back towards criticising the Soviet Union more heavily, suggesting post-revisionism was not the final or most accurate interpretation and that even its even-handedness has since been questioned.

Indicative content:
- Election manipulation was a key method used to establish communist control across Eastern Europe. In Hungary, the 1947 election was rigged by the USSR to favour communists, even though the 1945 free election had returned a mostly non-communist result. Similarly, in Romania, the 1946 elections were falsified to secure a communist victory, and in Poland, the 1947 elections were manipulated by Soviet-backed communists to undermine the coalition government.
- In Czechoslovakia, the Czech Communist Party won many votes in the 1946 election and then used political pressure to drive non-communists from power by 1948, ending democracy — showing that election manipulation was a sustained and widespread tool of Soviet control.
- However, the secret police were equally important in establishing control. In Hungary, the secret police — controlled by communists — suppressed opposition independently of elections, intimidating and removing rivals outside the electoral process.
- Political purges and other non-electoral methods also played a significant role. In Romania, King Michael was forced to abdicate following show trials against opponents, and in Bulgaria, the communist coalition of 1945 purged the opposition and abolished the monarchy, creating a communist constitution without relying solely on electoral fraud.

- The Western powers faced significant limitations during the crisis, as West Berlin remained entirely dependent on Soviet-controlled territory for food and vital resources, and breaking the Soviet military blockade of roads and railway links by force risked causing an outright war, meaning the airlift was born of weakness as much as strength.

- Despite widespread criticism, the USA did not intervene in Czechoslovakia and the US-Soviet relationship was not fundamentally damaged, suggesting that the doctrine's impact was limited when it came to superpower relations and the broader Cold War balance of power.
- Latin American nations such as Fidel Castro's Cuba generally continued to support Soviet action, and although Mexico broke away, this was described as not hugely significant, indicating that the damage to Soviet influence in some regions was relatively minor.

The Kapp Putsch of March 1920, led by Wolfgang Kapp, saw Freikorps forces attempt to overthrow the government entirely, forcing it to flee Berlin.

- The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, passed by Congress on 7th August 1964, gave President Johnson sweeping powers to respond to further attacks without a formal declaration of war, suggesting the incident was treated as serious enough to warrant significant military authority.

- The USA had provoked tension in the region by using its ships to allow ARVN troops to conduct raids on the North along the Gulf of Tonkin, meaning the North's hostility was partly a reaction to prior US-backed aggression rather than an unprovoked act of war.

- Britain and France had strategic reasons to avoid alienating Mussolini completely, as shown by the Stresa Front of 1935, in which all three countries agreed to unite against Hitler; this meant the League's member states faced genuine diplomatic pressure that complicated a stronger response to the invasion of Abyssinia.

Indicative content:
- The Warsaw Pact was explicitly formed in 1955 as a direct reaction to NATO, suggesting it was primarily defensive in purpose; Khrushchev presented it as a collective security measure to protect Eastern Bloc nations from Western military threats.
- The Warsaw Pact was signed by eight nations including the Soviet Union, East Germany, Poland, and Czechoslovakia, giving the appearance of a multilateral defensive alliance comparable to NATO's structure in the West.
- The Warsaw Pact also served to extend and consolidate Soviet political and military dominance over Eastern Europe, functioning as a tool of control rather than purely defence, since member states had little genuine independence from Moscow.
- The Warsaw Pact complemented other Soviet-led structures such as Comecon and Cominform, suggesting it was part of a broader Soviet strategy to bind Eastern Bloc nations economically and politically to the USSR, going beyond a simple defensive military response to NATO.

Indicative content:
- The Yalta Conference produced significant agreements on the future of Nazi Germany, including demilitarisation, the trial of Nazi war criminals, and a shared system of occupation zones, showing the Grand Alliance could cooperate on major decisions about the defeated power.
- The conference also saw the creation of the United Nations in February 1945, replacing the failed League of Nations with a new international body designed to maintain peace and prevent future global conflicts, which was a significant shared achievement.
- However, agreements over Eastern Europe were an uneasy compromise rather than a true success; Stalin promised free elections in Poland but later broke this promise, meaning the Yalta agreements failed to secure genuine democratic freedoms in liberated countries.
- Tensions over reparations also revealed limits to agreement — Stalin demanded $20 billion in monetary reparations from Germany, but no firm monetary figure was agreed, leaving this issue unresolved and a source of ongoing friction between the USSR and its allies.

Indicative content:
- The armaments clauses did humiliate Germany because the German army was reduced to just 100,000 men with no tanks, stripping Germany of the powerful military the country had been proud of under Kaiser leadership, making the restrictions deeply embarrassing for the nation.
- Germany was also forbidden from having an air force and its navy was cut to just 15,000 men and 6 battleships with no submarines, reducing a once-mighty military power to near-insignificance and adding to the sense of national shame.
- However, the armaments clauses also had a clear security purpose: the restrictions were intended to ensure Germany could not launch another offensive war, as its forces would only be large enough to act as a defensive army if attacked, protecting the other Allied nations from future aggression.
- The clause limiting Germany to a defensive army only, with restrictions negotiated at the Palace of Versailles in 1919, reflected the genuine fear among the Allies that an unrestricted German military would again threaten the peace of Europe, suggesting the motive was security as much as humiliation.

- The Anschluss ban also meant Germany could not strengthen itself by merging with Austria, leaving it weakened at a time when 13% of German land and 6 million German-speaking people had already been stripped away by the treaty.

- The loss of Alsace-Lorraine to France and the handing over of the Saar with its coal fields struck at Germany's economic capacity and national pride in ways that many Germans felt on a daily basis, suggesting these losses caused more immediate and widespread humiliation than the Anschluss ban.

- The economic merger of the British and American zones into Bizonia deepened the ideological divide, since the Western zones were run as capitalist economies using free trade, in direct contrast to the Soviet zone which was organised along communist lines.

- The North Vietnamese had a strong cultural and geographical advantage because they knew the landscape, culture and language of the South, allowing them to operate effectively in enemy territory and blend in with the local population, making it very difficult for US forces to identify and combat them.
- The tunnel system developed during the war with the French gave North Vietnamese fighters a significant geographical advantage, allowing them to move troops and supplies secretly, launch surprise attacks, and shelter from US bombing campaigns, severely limiting the effectiveness of American military power.
- The political and economic support from China and the USSR, who sent $3 billion in aid, weapons and equipment between 1954 and 1967, was a crucial factor in sustaining the North Vietnamese war effort, suggesting strengths beyond geography and culture alone.
- The Ho Chi Minh Trail, running through Laos and Cambodia, allowed North Vietnam to supply the Viet Cong (VC) in the South continuously, and the USA could do little to stop this without risking wider wars, meaning political and logistical factors also played a major role in US failure.

Indicative content:
- The currency reform of 20 June 1948 was the immediate trigger of the Berlin Blockade. The Western Allies introduced the Deutschmark in Operation 'Bird Dog', replacing the devalued Military mark. The Soviets rejected this change and it directly provoked their decision to blockade the city.
- The currency reform increased West Berlin's prosperity, partly through Marshall Plan funding from the Americans, making the Western zone visibly wealthier. This threatened Soviet authority in their zone of Berlin, giving Stalin further reason to act by blockading the city to cut West Berlin off from the West.
- However, the blockade can also be seen as a Soviet response to longer-term US provocation. The Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan had already heightened Cold War tensions before the currency reform, suggesting the blockade had deeper causes beyond the immediate currency change.
- Stalin also introduced his own currency, the East German mark, in response to the Allied reform, suggesting his primary motivation was to stamp down USSR authority over his zone rather than being provoked solely by the Deutschmark itself. This points to an underlying struggle for control of Berlin that pre-dated the currency reform.

- Italy left the League of Nations in May 1937, further reducing the number of powerful member states and leaving only Great Britain, France, and the USSR as significant powers, which severely undermined the League's credibility and reach.
- The self-interest of Great Britain and France played a significant role in the League's collapse, as both nations proved unwilling to prioritise the protection of other countries over their own domestic and imperial concerns, making collective security unworkable in practice.
- Even with Japan and Italy still present, the League of Nations had structural weaknesses rooted in the self-interest of its remaining major powers, suggesting the League's failure stemmed from deeper political unwillingness rather than membership losses alone.

Indicative content:
- Truman feared the domino effect, believing that as more nations gained communist governments, they would fund populist uprisings in neighbouring countries, causing communism to spread rapidly across Eastern Europe and the Middle East, making intervention through containment urgent.
- By 1947, communist parties supported by the USSR were already in control of Poland, Romania and Bulgaria, providing concrete evidence that the domino effect was already underway and strengthening Truman's case for a policy of containment.
- Winston Churchill's 'Iron Curtain' speech of March 1946 had already framed the threat as a divided Europe, suggesting that Truman's decision to pursue containment was also shaped by allied pressure and the broader ideological framing of the conflict rather than the domino effect alone.
- Truman also committed to containment for economic reasons, believing that providing financial and economic aid through the Marshall Plan would make communism less attractive to war-damaged populations, indicating that long-term economic strategy was a separate and significant motive.

- Fear of a communist election victory encouraged Eisenhower to back Diem when he refused to hold elections in 1956 as required by the Geneva Accords, showing that containing communism at all costs was central to US decision-making.
- However, growing instability caused by Diem's weak and corrupt government also drew the USA deeper in, as Diem's favouring of Catholics over the Buddhist majority and his neglect of rural villagers fuelled widespread opposition that threatened the south's survival.
- The rise of the Vietcong and the formation of the National Liberation Front (NLF), supported by North Vietnam via the Ho Chi Minh Trail from 1959, created a direct military threat that forced Eisenhower to send advisors to train the ARVN, pulling the USA further into the conflict beyond ideological concerns alone.

- The Cold War context intensified fears of communism, with the Vietnam War seen as a 'flashpoint' in the wider struggle against the USSR. Americans worried that allowing Vietnam to fall to communism could spread the threat closer to home.

Indicative content:

- Veterans openly campaigning about the atrocities they had witnessed in Vietnam gave the opposition movement credibility and moral weight, making it harder for the government to justify continuing the war to the broader American public.
